verses.note: Abram's wealth is real and is counted among God's blessings in later chapters (24:35), but this chapter shows at once that it brings pressure and conflict. Scripture treats possessions as gifts that must be held loosely, and the next verses show Abram doing exactly that.

Lot chose land by what his eyes saw (13:10), and the wealth he gathered there is the first thing he loses. The verse shows, without comment, how exposed a life becomes when its choices are made for gain.
Abram's tenth is the Bible's first tithe, given freely before any law required it. It is a confession that the spoils came from God; Jacob will make a similar vow in 28:22.
The servant presents Abraham's wealth not as achievement but as blessing: the LORD gave it. Scripture consistently treats riches as a gift held under God, as Deuteronomy 8:18 later reminds Israel.

Isaac's wealth is presented as a gift of the LORD, not an achievement, yet it immediately brings envy and conflict. The verse neither despises prosperity nor treats it as safe; blessing in the land still has to be lived out among resentful neighbors.

Jacob's tithe begins from the conviction that everything he will have is God's gift: ‘of all that You give me’. The tenth is a return of part of what is already received, which is how the rest of Scripture frames giving (1 Chronicles 29:14).

Jesus does not condemn possessions as such but storing them as a person's security. Wealth kept on earth is exposed to decay and loss; ‘treasure in heaven’ is what is given and done for God, which he keeps.
The saying treats generosity as a matter of sight: the way a person looks at money reveals and shapes the whole self. Greed is not only a wrong act but a darkness that spreads.
Luke sets the saying after the parable of the shrewd manager and adds that the lovers of money scoffed (Luke 16:13-14). The issue in both Gospels is allegiance, not the amount a person owns.

Wealth is named as one of the forces that choke the word, and Mark's word for it, apatē, calls it deceitful: it promises what it cannot give. The story of the rich man in 10:17-27 shows this thorn at work.

Jesus does not make selling everything a universal rule in Mark (Levi keeps a house in 2:15), but he identifies what stands between this man and following him and asks for it. Wealth here is not neutral; it can be the thing a person cannot give up, and the command to give to the poor ties discipleship to justice for them. Clement of Alexandria's sermon Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? read the command as renouncing the passions attached to wealth; Antony of Egypt, according to Athanasius's Life of Antony (2), heard it literally and gave his property away.

Jesus does not say riches are sinful, but that they make entry into the kingdom humanly impossible, because they supply the security that the kingdom asks a person to give up. The disciples' shock shows how deeply they assumed wealth meant God's favor.

God measures giving by what it costs the giver. The widow gives what the rich man of chapter 10 could not, everything, and the placement invites comparison. Addison Wright (The Widow's Mites: Praise or Lament?, Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1982) argued that in context Jesus laments a system that took a widow's living just before the temple's fall; the traditional reading hears praise of her devotion. The chapter note sets out both; many hold them together.

The rich are ‘sent away empty’, not because wealth is evil but because the self-sufficient have no room to receive. Luke develops this in the parable of the rich fool (12:16-21) and the rich ruler (18:18-25).
Repentance for a tax collector means honesty in the very work that tempts him. John addresses money at the point where a person earns it.
Possessions are held for the sake of others' need. Luke does not command a single economic system, but he shows the Spirit loosening believers' grip on property.

They accepted the loss of property with joy because they knew they had a better and lasting possession. The verse relativizes earthly goods not by despising them but by setting them beside what cannot be taken.

The beast's power reaches ordinary buying and selling. The verses expose how economic participation can require loyalty to a false god, and they ask believers to count faithfulness worth its cost in livelihood, as the letters to Thyatira and Laodicea already did.
